fixes.explanation: That's the one. Jesus asks, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” The passage doesn't spell out what “these” means, so I'll leave it open too. Simon Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, hears this question once breakfast is over. I think a question that short and that direct makes a man stand up straight.

Nothing about fishing comes out of Jesus' mouth here. Breakfast is done, and He asks, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” That question is about love, not nets. I've had plenty of conversations that went around the block before getting to the point.

That's it. The text says Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “…do you love Me…” Peter doesn't storm off, though. He answers, “Lord, You know all things…” and, “You know I love You.”
Amusement isn't the feeling in the text, baker. The passage says Peter was deeply hurt by the third question. Even so, he answers Jesus honestly: “You know I love You.”

That's right. Jesus says someone else will dress Peter and lead him “…where you do not want to go.” It's a quiet line with a lot packed in. Jesus says that when Peter was young, he dressed himself and walked where he wanted. I think this is one of the heavier parts of the passage, so take it slow.

That's the opposite of what Jesus says. When Peter is old, someone else will dress him and lead him where he does not want to go. The young Peter is the one who walked where he wanted. I think this is one of the heavier lines in the passage.

Yes. The writer explains that Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. We're told right there what the words are pointing to. It's a heavy thing to hear, and I won't joke about it. Then Jesus says to Peter, “Follow Me.”

It's true. The text says Jesus said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. So the words about old age aren't random. The text tells us what they point to. It's a heavy moment, and right after it Jesus tells Peter, “Follow Me.”
Peter doesn't ask for anybody to join them. He sees the other disciple following and asks, “Lord, what about him?” The text doesn't say what Peter had in mind, so I won't guess.

Right. The rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die. The brothers here are fellow believers. The rumor grew out of Jesus' answer, and the text sets it straight right away. Rumors move like cookie crumbs: one bump of the counter and they're everywhere.

Marriage never comes up in this passage. The rumor among the brothers was that this disciple would not die. That's a much bigger claim than a wedding. It took off from Jesus' answer to Peter, and the text corrects it in the very next line.

Preaching isn't what the rumor was about. The text says the rumor among the brothers was that this disciple would not die. The brothers here are fellow believers. It grew out of what Jesus said to Peter, and the text corrects it right there.

That's right. The text says plainly that Jesus did not say this disciple would not die. He said only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” Notice the “if” in His words. It's a small word, but it's holding up that whole sentence.

Peter is the one Jesus was talking to, but he's not the one the passage names as the writer. Verse 24 points to the disciple whom Jesus loved, the one Peter asked about. Peter asked the questions here, and that other disciple is the one who testifies and wrote these things down.

Thomas, called Didymus, is one of the disciples listed on the beach with the others (John 21:2). But this passage never names him as the writer. Verse 24 says the one who testifies and wrote these things down is the disciple whom Jesus loved.
